questions.stem: The solution for the inequality \(\frac{3}{x-1}\lt 5\) can be expressed as:
questions.hint: Find x = 8/5 (equality) and x = 1 (undefined), then test each region or sketch.

steps.explain: Find where the two sides are equal and where the left side is undefined.
Sketch \(y=\frac{3}{x-1}\) and \(y=5\). The hyperbola is below the line for \(x\lt 1\) (where it is negative) and for \(x\gt\frac85\).
The inequality is strict and \(x=1\) is excluded, so both ends are open.
Multiplying both sides by \(x-1\) without care loses the \(x\lt 1\) part (options A, C).

keyPoints.note: Don't multiply by x − 1 (its sign is unknown). Use the critical values x = 1 and x = 8/5.

questions.hint: Multiply by (3x + 1)² (always positive), factorise, and exclude x = −1/3.

steps.explain: \(x\neq-\frac13\). Multiply both sides by the square \((3x+1)^2\), which is positive, so the inequality keeps its direction.
Bring everything to one side and factorise.
Critical values \(x=-\frac13\) and \(x=1\); the parabola is positive outside them.
\(x=-\frac13\) makes the original undefined, so exclude it.

keyPoints.note: Multiply both sides by the square of the denominator so the sign doesn't flip.

questions.hint: Critical values −2, 0, 2; test each interval; exclude x = 0.

steps.explain: Critical values: numerator zero at \(x=\pm2\); denominator zero at \(x=0\) (excluded).
Test a value in each interval.
Keep the intervals where the expression is \(\ge0\). Include \(x=\pm2\) (value 0) but not \(x=0\) (undefined).

keyPoints.note: Use the critical values x = ±2 and x = 0, then test signs.

questions.stem: The graph of \(y=f(x)\) is shown. Which features must the graph of \(y=\frac1{f(x)}\) have?
questions.hint: The reciprocal is undefined where the original function is zero; it is zero only where the original function is unbounded.

keyPoints.note: Read the original graph’s vertical asymptote and x-intercept first.
Zeros of f become vertical asymptotes; vertical asymptotes of f are not zeros of 1/f.

steps.explain: The given graph is a logarithmic-shaped curve: it has a vertical asymptote at x=0 and crosses the x-axis at x=1.
Where f(x)=0, its reciprocal is undefined and becomes unbounded.
As x approaches 0 from the right, f(x) becomes very negative, so 1/f(x) approaches 0 from below.

questions.solution: Graph A: The reciprocal has a vertical asymptote where f(x)=0 at x=1, and approaches 0 at both domain ends.

parts.hint: Reflect the negative part of y = x² − 2x − 4 up, then take reciprocals: zeros → asymptotes.

steps.explain: First take the absolute value: the part of the parabola below the \(x\)-axis (between \(1\pm\sqrt5\)) is reflected up, so the vertex becomes \((1,5)\).
Now take the reciprocal. Zeros of \(f\) become vertical asymptotes; large values become small (\(y\to0\) as \(x\to\pm\infty\)); the maximum 5 in the middle becomes a minimum \(\frac15\).
The whole graph is above the \(x\)-axis.

parts.answer: Take |f| (reflect the part below the x-axis), then the reciprocal: vertical asymptotes at \(x=1\pm\sqrt5\) (zeros of f), horizontal asymptote y = 0, local minimum \(\left(1,\frac15\right)\) from the vertex, y-intercept \(\frac14\); the graph is always positive, rising to infinity at both asymptotes.

keyPoints.note: Zeros of x² − 2x − 4 become vertical asymptotes; the turning value 5 becomes 1/5.

questions.stem:
The diagram below is a sketch of the graph of the function \(y=f(x)\).

\(f(x)=\frac{2}{x+1}+4\)

Draw a separate half-page graph of each of the following functions, showing all asymptotes and intercepts.

parts.hint: |f| reflects only the negative parts upward.

steps.explain: Where \(f(x)\lt 0\) (between \(x=-1.5\) and \(x=-1\)), reflect in the \(x\)-axis; elsewhere unchanged.

parts.answer: Reflect the part below the x-axis (for −1.5 < x < −1) upwards. Asymptotes x = −1, y = 4; touches the x-axis at (−1.5, 0); y-intercept 6.

keyPoints.note: Flip the part below the x-axis; nothing else changes.

parts.hint: Keep x ≥ 0 and reflect it in the y-axis.

steps.explain: For \(x\ge0\) the graph is unchanged; for \(x\lt0\) use the mirror image of the right half. The left branch and \(x=-1\) disappear.
Result: even graph, peak \((0,6)\), asymptote \(y=4\) on both sides.

parts.answer: Keep the part for x ≥ 0 (from (0, 6) down towards y = 4) and reflect it in the y-axis. Asymptote y = 4 only; maximum point (0, 6); no x-intercepts and no vertical asymptote.

keyPoints.note: f(|x|) is even: copy the right-hand half onto the left.

parts.hint: Reciprocal: zeros ↔ vertical asymptotes; y = 4 → y = 1/4.

steps.explain: Simplify: \(f(x)=\frac{4x+6}{x+1}\), so \(\frac{1}{f(x)}=\frac{x+1}{4x+6}\).
Zeros of \(f\) become vertical asymptotes; vertical asymptotes of \(f\) become zeros; \(y=4\) becomes \(y=\frac14\).

parts.answer: \(\frac{1}{f(x)}=\frac{x+1}{4x+6}\): vertical asymptote x = −1.5 (zero of f), horizontal asymptote y = 1/4, x-intercept (−1, 0) (where f → ∞), y-intercept 1/6.

keyPoints.note: Where f = 0 you get an asymptote; where f → ∞ you get a zero.

parts.hint: Take ±√f where f ≥ 0; y = 4 becomes y = ±2.

steps.explain: \(y=\pm\sqrt{f(x)}\) exists only where \(f(x)\ge0\): \(x\le-1.5\) or \(x\gt-1\).
Asymptotes: \(y=4\to y=\pm2\); \(x=-1\) stays. Intercepts: \(y=\pm\sqrt6\) and \((-1.5,0)\) with a vertical tangent.

parts.answer: \(y=\pm\sqrt{f(x)}\) where f ≥ 0, i.e. x ≤ −1.5 or x > −1. Horizontal asymptotes y = ±2, vertical asymptote x = −1, y-intercepts ±√6, vertical tangent at (−1.5, 0). Symmetric in the x-axis; nothing for −1.5 < x < −1.

keyPoints.note: Only where f(x) ≥ 0; mirror the √f curve in the x-axis.

questions.stem:
The diagram shows the graph of \(y=f(x)\).

Draw sketches of the graphs of the following on separate number planes:

parts.hint: Keep the x ≥ 0 part and reflect it in the y-axis.

steps.explain: For \(x\ge0\), \(|x|=x\), so the graph is unchanged on the right of the \(y\)-axis.
For \(x\lt 0\), \(f(|x|)=f(-x)\): the right-hand half is reflected in the \(y\)-axis. The original left part (and \(x=-1\)) is thrown away.
Key features: \((0,1)\), zeros at \(x=\pm\frac12\), asymptote \(y=2\) on both sides.

parts.answer: Keep the part of y = f(x) for x ≥ 0 (through (0, 1), down to (1/2, 0), then up towards y = 2) and reflect it in the y-axis. The result is even: zeros at x = ±1/2, y-intercept 1, horizontal asymptote y = 2 on both sides; the part for x < 0 (including the asymptote x = −1) is discarded.

keyPoints.note: f(|x|) is even: copy the right-hand half onto the left.

parts.hint: y = ±√f(x): only where f ≥ 0; points with f = 0 or 1 stay put; y → ±√2.

steps.explain: \(y^2=f(x)\) means \(y=\pm\sqrt{f(x)}\). This only exists where \(f(x)\ge0\): for \(x\gt -1\). The branch for \(x\lt -1\) (where \(f\lt 0\)) disappears.
Invariant points: where \(f=0\) or \(f=1\), \(\sqrt f=f\). So \((\frac12,0)\) and \((0,1)\) stay; \((0,-1)\) is the mirror image.
Asymptotes: \(f\to2\) gives \(y\to\pm\sqrt2\); \(f\to\infty\) near \(x=-1\) keeps the vertical asymptote. Square-rooting lifts values between 0 and 1 and lowers values above 1.
Reflect the top half in the \(x\)-axis. At \((\frac12,0)\) the curve has a vertical tangent.

parts.answer: \(y=\pm\sqrt{f(x)}\), only where f(x) ≥ 0, i.e. for x > −1. Points where f = 0 or 1 stay fixed: (1/2, 0), (0, ±1). Asymptotes: x = −1 (both branches go to ±∞) and y = ±√2. The graph is symmetric about the x-axis and has vertical tangents at (1/2, 0). Nothing for x < −1.

keyPoints.note: Take ±√f(x) where f(x) ≥ 0. Asymptote y = 2 becomes y = ±√2.

questions.hint: Use the |x| symmetry first, then the period of sin 2x.

steps.explain: \(y=\pm\sqrt{3\sin|2x|}\): the graph exists only where \(\sin|2x|\ge0\), and it is symmetric about the \(x\)-axis (closed loops).
\(|2x|\) makes the graph symmetric about the \(y\)-axis: there must be loops on both sides of the origin touching at \(O\). That leaves B or D.
\(\sin2x\) has period \(\pi\) and is positive for \(0\lt x\lt\frac\pi2\), so each loop is \(\frac\pi2\) wide (from 0 to \(\frac\pi2\), then \(\pi\) to \(\frac{3\pi}{2}\)).
Only D has loops of width \(\frac\pi2\) on both sides of the origin. (B has width \(\pi\), which is \(\sin|x|\).)

keyPoints.note: |2x| gives y-axis symmetry; sin 2x has period π, so each loop is π/2 wide.

questions.stem: The graph of \(y=\cos^{-1}x\) is transformed to a graph whose endpoints are \((-9,\pi)\) and \((-3,0)\). Find its equation.
questions.hint: For inverse cosine, the basic endpoints are \((1,0)\) and \((-1,\pi)\). Match these to the transformed endpoints.

keyPoints.note: The basic graph has endpoints (1, 0) and (−1, π).

steps.explain: The transformed graph has y=0 when x=−3 and y=π when x=−9. Thus the inverse-cosine input must be 1 at x=−3 and −1 at x=−9.
The linear input that satisfies these endpoint values has slope \(\frac{1-(-1)}{-3-(-9)}=\frac{1}{3}\).
Substitute this input into the inverse cosine.

parts.stem: Explain why the domain of the function \(f(x)\) must be restricted if \(f(x)\) is to have an inverse functions.
parts.hint: An inverse function needs f to be one-to-one (horizontal line test).

steps.explain: \(f(x)=x^2-4x+3=(x-2)^2-1\) is a parabola. Most horizontal lines cut it twice (e.g. \(f(1)=f(3)=0\)).
When \(x\) and \(y\) are swapped, each such \(x\) would have two \(y\)-values, so the inverse would not be a function. Restricting the domain (e.g. \(x\ge2\)) makes \(f\) one-to-one.

options: Because \(f\) is undefined for some values of \(x\).
Because \(f\) is not one-to-one: a horizontal line can cut the parabola twice, so swapping \(x\) and \(y\) would give two \(y\)-values for one \(x\).

keyPoints.note: Use the horizontal line test on the parabola.

parts.stem: Find the equation of the inverse function \(f^{-1}(x)\) if the domain of \(f(x)\) is restricted to \(x\ge2\).
parts.hint: Complete the square, swap x and y, keep the root that gives y ≥ 2.

steps.explain: Complete the square.
Swap \(x\) and \(y\); now \(y\ge2\).
Since \(y\ge2\), take the positive root.

keyPoints.note: The inverse's range is x ≥ 2, so choose the + square root.

parts.stem: State the domain and range of \(f^{-1}(x)\), given the restriction in part ii).
parts.hint: Domain and range swap between f and f⁻¹.

steps.explain: The domain of \(f^{-1}\) is the range of \(f\): with \(x\ge2\), \(f(x)=(x-2)^2-1\ge-1\).
The range of \(f^{-1}\) is the domain of \(f\).
Check with the formula: \(\sqrt{x+1}\) needs \(x\ge-1\), and \(2+\sqrt{x+1}\ge2\) ✓.

keyPoints.note: Domain of f⁻¹ = range of f; range of f⁻¹ = domain of f.

parts.stem: On the same diagram, sketch the graphs of \(y=f(x)\) and \(y=f^{-1}(x)\), showing clearly the coordinates of the end points and the intercepts on the coordinate axes.
parts.hint: Reflect the restricted parabola in y = x; swap the coordinates of key points.

steps.explain: \(y=f(x)\) for \(x\ge2\): the right half of the parabola, starting at the vertex \((2,-1)\) (closed dot) and crossing the \(x\)-axis at \(x=3\).
\(y=f^{-1}(x)\) is the reflection in \(y=x\): end point \((-1,2)\), \(y\)-intercept \(f^{-1}(0)=2+1=3\).
The two graphs are mirror images in \(y=x\) and intersect on that line.

parts.answer: y = f(x), x ≥ 2: right half of the parabola from the end point (2, −1), crossing the x-axis at (3, 0). y = f⁻¹(x): its reflection in y = x, from (−1, 2), crossing the y-axis at (0, 3). The two curves meet on y = x.

keyPoints.note: Each key point (a, b) on f becomes (b, a) on f⁻¹.

questions.stem: The function \(f(x)=1+\ln x\) is defined in the domain \((0,1]\).

steps.explain: Apply the product rule \((uv)\prime=u\prime v+uv\prime\) with \(u=x\) and \(v=\ln x\).
Simplify the second product.

parts.stem:
The diagram shows the graphs of the function \(y=f(x)\) and the inverse function \(y=f^{-1}(x)\).

Find in simplest exact form the area of the shaded region in the first quadrant bounded by the curves \(y=f(x)\), \(y=f^{-1}(x)\) and the coordinate axes.
parts.hint: Use the symmetry in y = x: find the half below y = x and double it.

steps.explain: The graphs of a function and its inverse reflect across \(y=x\). They meet at \((1,1)\), so this diagonal divides the shaded region into two equal areas. Work out the lower half first.
steps.work: \(f(1)=1+\ln1=1\Rightarrow f^{-1}(1)=1;\quad y=x\text{ is the symmetry line}\)

steps.explain: The lower half is the triangle with vertices \((0,0),(1,0),(1,1)\), with the area under \(y=f(x)\) from its x-intercept to 1 removed. Find that intercept.
Use the antiderivative established in part (i) to find the area under \(f\) on this interval.
Subtract this curved area from the triangle area to obtain one half of the shaded region.
Double the half-area because of inverse symmetry.

keyPoints.text: the area of the shaded region
keyPoints.note: f and f⁻¹ are mirror images in y = x, so the region is symmetric about that line.

parts.stem: Sketch the graph of the curve \(y=\frac{1}{f(x)}\), showing clearly the coordinates of the endpoints and the equations of any asymptotes.
parts.hint: f = 0 at x = 1/e gives a vertical asymptote; check x → 0⁺ and x = 1.

steps.explain: Find where the denominator \(f(x)=1+\ln x\) is zero. The reciprocal is undefined there and has a vertical asymptote.
Check the limit at the open end of the domain.
Find the included endpoint and determine the sign of each branch.

Check the direction of each branch: the derivative is negative throughout its domain, so both branches decrease as x increases. Sketch with vertical asymptote \(x=1/e\), open approach to \((0,0)\), and the included endpoint \((1,1)\).

parts.answer: \(y=\frac{1}{1+\ln x}\) on (0, 1]: vertical asymptote x = 1/e (where f = 0); as x → 0⁺, f → −∞ so y → 0⁻ (open endpoint at the origin); for 0 < x < 1/e the curve is negative, decreasing to −∞; for 1/e < x ≤ 1 it comes down from +∞ to the endpoint (1, 1).

keyPoints.text: Sketch the graph of the curve
keyPoints.note: Zeros of f become vertical asymptotes of 1/f.

parts.stem: Use interval notation to state the range of the function \(y=\frac{1}{f(x)}\)
parts.hint: Split at x = 1/e: negative branch, then the branch ending at (1, 1).

steps.explain: For \(0\lt x\lt\frac1e\): \(f\) takes all negative values, so \(\frac1f\) takes all values in \((-\infty,0)\) (never 0 itself).
For \(\frac1e\lt x\le1\): \(0\lt f\le1\), so \(\frac1f\ge1\), with 1 reached at \(x=1\).
Combine.

keyPoints.note: 1/f is never 0; the right branch includes its endpoint value 1.

questions.stem: Given that \(f(x)=e^x-1\) and \(y=f^{-1}(x)\), find an expression for \(\frac{dy}{dx}\).
questions.hint: First find the inverse by swapping x and y in y=e^x−1, then differentiate the inverse.

keyPoints.note: Focus on this information from the question when choosing the method and carrying out the calculation.

steps.explain: Start with y=f(x).
Swap x and y because the inverse reverses input and output.
Add 1, then take ln of both sides to isolate y.
Differentiate the inverse and note its domain.

questions.stem: Which of the following pairs of parametric equations represents a circle that passes through the origin?
questions.hint: The radius must equal the distance from the centre (3, 4) to the origin.

steps.explain: Identify the circle represented by the parametric equations.
A circle passes through the origin exactly when its radius equals the distance from its centre to the origin.
Select the option whose radius is 5.
Verify that this circle actually includes the origin by choosing the direction from its centre to the origin.

keyPoints.note: Centre (3, 4) to (0, 0) is 5 units — that must be the radius.
